How long should retirement savings last? Read the survival curve

Explore preliminary Canadian life-table statistics alongside separate funding scenarios that show the cost of planning for more years.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

The central idea

An average remaining lifetime is a population summary. A retirement funding horizon must also consider the consequences of living longer than that average.

01

Know what the statistical curve represents

The first two graphics use Statistics Canada’s Canada-level 2022–2024 period life table, released on 13 January 2026. The source marks this period preliminary because late death registrations can lead to revisions. The chart preserves the publisher’s Males and Females categories.

A period table summarizes a pattern of mortality for a reference period. It is not a forecast that follows today’s 65-year-olds through future changes in mortality. Its survivor counts describe a synthetic cohort, rather than a survey sample of the people now shown on the age axis.

Each survival line starts at 100% at age 65. Later points divide the source’s survivor count at that age by its survivor count at 65, within the same sex category: conditional survival = lx ÷ l65. This conditioning matters because the comparison begins with people who have already reached 65.

02

Read the birthdays beyond the average

The published remaining life expectancy at 65 is 19.43 years for Males and 22.15 for Females in this preliminary table. Those are averages under the period’s mortality pattern. They do not mean that everyone dies at the average age or that half the group necessarily lives beyond it.

The milestone bars show derived survival shares to 85, 90 and 95, conditional on reaching 65. For example, the age-90 shares are about 29.14% and 42.00% for the respective source categories. The data table retains the displayed percentages, and the source link identifies the original survivor counts and reference period.

These population patterns provide context for a long funding horizon. They do not adjust for an individual’s health, family history or future circumstances. They also do not calculate the chance that at least one member of a couple survives. Household joint-survival analysis requires additional assumptions and should not be inferred by adding the two percentages.

03

Keep the funding scenarios separate from the statistics

The controls change the hypothetical funding illustrations only. They do not alter the official life-table observations. Enter the annual spending shortfall after other income, the years it needs to be funded, a real return assumption and the capital allocated to that need.

The model funds a level shortfall in today’s purchasing-power dollars, paid at each year-end. For annual gap G, real return r and n years, the reserve is G[1 − (1 + r)−n] ÷ r. At zero return, it is G × n. A negative real return increases the starting reserve required for the same future purchasing power.

The default CAD 20,000 annual gap for 30 years at an assumed 2% real return requires CAD 447,929.11 today. After CAD 400,000 of allocated capital, the modeled gap is CAD 47,929.11. These are deterministic calculations, with constant returns and no market sequence, taxes or fees beyond what is already assumed in the real rate.

04

Use longer horizons as a resilience test

The grouped bars compare the funding requirement for 20, 25, 30 and 35 years with the same capital allocation. The matrix varies both the horizon and real return. Each cell reports additional capital needed, with zero as a floor when allocated capital already covers the modeled requirement.

A zero cell is not a probability of success. The calculation assumes the selected return occurs smoothly and the shortfall remains constant in real terms. Different inflation exposure, investment losses, care needs or other spending could change the required payments.

The model does not multiply each year’s essential spending by the chance of surviving to that year. Such weighting would describe a different expected-value question. It would not demonstrate that one household can fund every payment if it lives longer. Risk pooling, annuities and insurance require their own pricing, contract and suitability analysis.

05

Connect longevity to an income plan

List the spending that continues if retirement lasts longer, and the income sources that continue alongside it. Check their terms, inflation treatment and any changes after a spouse or partner dies. Keep dependable cash flows distinct from assets that may need to be sold.

Test a longer funding period without simultaneously improving the return assumption. That exposes the cost of additional years. Then identify possible responses, such as different saving, spending, retirement timing or income arrangements, and assess their constraints in a fuller plan.

Revisit the horizon as circumstances and source estimates change. These charts combine dated population context with transparent arithmetic; they do not select a personal lifespan, establish a safe withdrawal rate or guarantee that a particular reserve will be sufficient.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Charts labelled “Official statistics” or “Derived from official statistics” identify their source periods. Other charts are hypothetical scenarios. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
